cells.tense: You are holding several open possibilities right now, and you can tell which one has the most to it.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin the open thing that has the most to it — smallest real first move, no plan standing in for the act, no end in sight.
cells.core:
You can see the shape of a thing before it has one. Turn that on a decision here — before a lane is picked, while everything is still spread out — and the options stay alive longer than they would otherwise. Somewhere in you this works best when something gets moving and the shape comes out of the motion. That's the part worth naming, because this is where possibility is supposed to breathe.

Do one of these on purpose. Begin the open thing that has the most to it — smallest real first move, no end in sight, no plan standing in for the act. Starting is what gives the spark something to land on, and the confidence in the rest follows the start rather than the other way round.

cells.tense: At this point you have already decided every open thing, and the deciding happens further out than the things themselves.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Name the open question you've carried longest and put one concrete step on it — no announcement, no second opinion, nothing to report back.
cells.core:
Nothing is allowed to stay open. Every option gets resolved the moment it arrives, so the reasoning is doing its work before the situation has asked for it, and what's left is a row of answers to questions nobody has asked yet. The speed is real. It's moving through possibility the way it moves through a finished problem, and the unfinished part — the part that wants to stay unpicked a little longer — keeps getting closed on arrival.

Here is the piece that settles it. Take the open question you've carried longest and put one concrete step on it, not the whole decision. The step is what makes things make sense in your presence again, and it does that by being small enough to actually happen rather than large enough to be right.

cells.tense: A possibility was set in front of you at some point, and you stayed on the near side of it.
cells.act: pursue the emotional truth with someone
cells.ask: Give an open possibility weight by speaking it to one other person — what it would mean, not the odds — and remain in that exchange past the first reply.
cells.core:
The door is behind you and you're at it. You can work out how a thing would unfold — the reasoning runs fine — but the working-out doesn't turn into being somewhere, so possibilities stay laid out and none of them gets a weight. More analysis won't do it. Thinking alone is what you keep bringing, and thinking is what keeps them light.

Say it instead. Describe an open possibility to another person — not the odds, what it would mean — and stay in that conversation past the first reply. Meaning held between two people has weight to it, and weight is what lets a possibility start to be something you could pick up.

cells.tense: You are steering an open situation right now and not counting it as steering.
cells.act: be present to their feeling without drowning in it
cells.ask: When an unfinished thing arrives from someone, set aside sorting it — hold their side of it as it is, near enough to feel it and not so near it becomes yours.
cells.core:
Where this is going, the room stays open longer for the people in it. The reasoning lays their options out clearly before anything is decided — that's the work — but ask and you'd say you're only being clear, only saying what's there. The hand is on it. Whatever makes a shared possibility clearer is yours, and it doesn't get filed as yours.

Try this instead. Let their feeling be theirs, close enough to meet it and far enough that it stays theirs. Sitting with what's in the room is what this actually does, and the difference between arranging someone and being with them is only knowing which one you're doing.
